name: Wave 2 week 3: evaluation sets, tool calling and agents, Azure and Fabric, insurance pricing, FHIR, stream joins and exactly-once

concepts.title: Building evaluation datasets and golden sets
concepts.kw: evaluation dataset golden set test set reference answers labelling guidelines annotators agreement edge cases synthetic questions held out regression suite versioning llm app
concepts.s: An evaluation dataset, or golden set, is a fixed list of realistic inputs with the answer or grading notes you expect. It lets you measure an LLM feature before and after every change instead of guessing.
concepts.d: Start from real traffic where you can: sample logged questions, remove personal data, and group them by category and difficulty so rare but important cases are not drowned out. Add edge cases written by experts, such as ambiguous questions, questions with no answer, and attempts to break the rules. Synthetic questions generated by a model can fill gaps, but a person should review each one. For every item, record the expected answer or a short rubric, plus any source passages. Write labelling guidelines and have two people label a sample to check they agree. Keep a held-out part you never tune prompts on, version the set like code, and add every serious production failure to it. Fifty to two hundred good items beat thousands of careless ones.
concepts.e: A support bot's golden set has 180 items: 120 sampled from last month's chats in 6 categories, 40 expert edge cases and 20 reviewed synthetic ones. Two reviewers agreed on 92% of labels, and 40 items are held out.
concepts.c: Why should part of an evaluation set be held out from prompt tuning?
concepts.i: Interviewers look for real sampled inputs, coverage of categories and edge cases, clear labelling rules with an agreement check, a held-out split and a habit of adding production failures.

concepts.title: Azure data services map
concepts.kw: azure data services map adls gen2 azure databricks synapse analytics microsoft fabric event hubs stream analytics cosmos db azure sql purview entra id key vault
concepts.s: Azure's data services cover storage, ingestion, processing, warehousing, streaming and governance. Knowing what each one does, and its AWS or Google Cloud match, lets you read any Azure job description.
concepts.d: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 is Blob storage with a hierarchical namespace, the base for most Azure lakes. Azure Data Factory builds and schedules copy and transformation pipelines. Azure Databricks runs Spark and Delta Lake, and Azure Synapse Analytics combines SQL pools, Spark and pipelines; Synapse is still supported, but Microsoft now steers new analytics work to Microsoft Fabric, a single software-as-a-service platform built on OneLake. Event Hubs ingests streams and speaks the Kafka protocol, and Stream Analytics runs SQL-like queries over them. Azure SQL Database and Cosmos DB are common sources. Microsoft Purview handles cataloguing and governance, Microsoft Entra ID handles identity, and Key Vault keeps secrets. Roughly, ADLS matches S3, Event Hubs matches Kinesis and Data Factory matches Glue plus Step Functions.
concepts.e: A retailer lands store sales from Azure SQL Database into ADLS Gen2 every hour with Data Factory, cleans them in Azure Databricks, streams 3,000 till events a second through Event Hubs and governs it all in Purview.
concepts.c: Which Azure service would you use as the storage layer for a data lake, and what makes it different from plain Blob storage?
concepts.i: Expect to map a pipeline to Azure services, explain where Synapse, Databricks and Fabric overlap, and give the AWS or Google Cloud equivalents. Mention identity and secrets, not only compute.

concepts.title: Insurance pricing and loss ratios for analysts
concepts.kw: insurance pricing loss ratio combined ratio expense ratio claim frequency severity pure premium burning cost rating factors glm poisson gamma exposure no claim bonus underwriting
concepts.s: Insurance pricing estimates what each policy is likely to cost in claims and adds expenses and margin. Loss ratios and combined ratios then show whether the prices were right.
concepts.d: The expected claims cost of a policy, the pure premium, is claim frequency times claim severity: how often claims happen per unit of exposure, and how much each costs on average. Actuaries model frequency with a Poisson GLM and severity with a gamma GLM, using rating factors such as vehicle age, city or sum insured, with exposure as an offset. Expenses, commission and profit are loaded on top. Afterwards, the loss ratio divides incurred claims (paid plus the change in reserves) by earned premium, and the combined ratio adds the expense ratio. A combined ratio above 100% means an underwriting loss before investment income. Some premiums are set by regulation rather than by each insurer, for example third-party motor cover in India, so check the rules before pricing.
concepts.e: A motor book has 50,000 policy-years of exposure, 4,000 claims and Rs 24 crore incurred. Frequency is 8%, severity Rs 60,000, so pure premium is Rs 4,800. On Rs 32 crore earned premium the loss ratio is 75%.
concepts.c: Why is the loss ratio worked out on earned premium and incurred claims rather than on cash received and cash paid?
concepts.i: Interviewers check that you can split cost into frequency and severity, define loss, expense and combined ratios, and explain why exposure and reserves matter. Mention GLMs and segment checks.

concepts.title: Stream joins and late data
concepts.kw: streaming stream-stream stream-static interval join temporal lookup watermark state late data outer null emission state store event time range condition side output impressions clicks
concepts.s: Joining streams means matching events that arrive at different times. The engine must keep unmatched events in state, so watermarks and time limits decide how long to wait and when to drop late data.
concepts.d: A stream-static join enriches each event from a table, such as a product lookup, and needs little state. A stream-stream join, such as impressions to clicks, must buffer both sides because a match may arrive later. Without limits that state grows forever, so you add a watermark on each side and a time-range condition, for example a click within 30 minutes of its impression. The engine can then drop buffered rows once the watermark passes. Outer joins only emit unmatched rows with nulls after the watermark moves past their window, so results are delayed. Flink offers interval joins for this and temporal joins that look up the version of a table valid at the event's time, such as a currency rate. Events later than the watermark are dropped or sent to a side output for correction.
concepts.e: Ad impressions and clicks join on ad_id with a 30-minute range and 10-minute watermarks. State holds about 40 minutes of events, roughly 2 GB, instead of growing by 50 GB a day without limits.
concepts.c: Why does a left outer stream-stream join emit its unmatched rows later than its matched rows?
concepts.i: Senior interviews ask how you bound state in stream-stream joins, what watermarks do to outer joins, and how you handle late events. Mention temporal joins for slowly changing lookups.

concepts.title: Structured outputs and function calling
concepts.kw: function calling tool calling structured outputs json schema strict mode constrained decoding arguments tool definition extraction validation pydantic tool result loop
concepts.s: Structured outputs make a model return JSON that fits a schema you give it. Function calling goes further: the model asks your code to run a named function with arguments, and you send back the result.
concepts.d: You describe each function with a name, a plain description and a JSON schema for its arguments. The model decides whether to call one and returns the name and arguments instead of prose. Your code runs it, for example a database lookup or a weather API, and passes the result back so the model can continue. Structured outputs use the same idea for answers: many providers can constrain the model so its output always matches the schema, often called strict mode. Even then, validate everything in code, for example with Pydantic, because a valid shape can still hold wrong values. Use enums, required fields and clear descriptions. Never let the model run arbitrary actions: allowlist functions, use read-only credentials where you can and ask a person before anything that changes data or spends money.
concepts.e: An invoice extractor asks for vendor, invoice_date, currency from an enum and line items with amounts. Strict mode removed 3% malformed JSON, and a Pydantic check that line items add up to the total caught another 1.5% of wrong values.
concepts.c: Why do you still validate a model's output in code when the provider guarantees it matches your JSON schema?
concepts.i: Expect to describe the call, execute and return loop, how schemas and enums reduce errors, and the guardrails you put around functions that read or change real data.

concepts.title: Microsoft Fabric for data engineers
concepts.kw: microsoft fabric onelake lakehouse warehouse sql analytics endpoint shortcuts mirroring data factory dataflow gen2 notebooks real-time intelligence eventhouse direct lake capacity units f sku smoothing
concepts.s: Microsoft Fabric is a software-as-a-service analytics platform: data engineering, warehousing, pipelines, real-time analytics and Power BI share one lake, OneLake, and one pool of paid capacity.
concepts.d: Each organisation gets one OneLake, built on ADLS Gen2, with workspaces as folders. A lakehouse stores files and Delta tables you work on with Spark notebooks, and gets a read-only SQL analytics endpoint; a warehouse gives full T-SQL over Delta tables. Data Factory in Fabric brings pipelines and Dataflow Gen2. Shortcuts point at data in ADLS, Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage without copying it, and mirroring keeps a near real-time copy of databases such as Azure SQL Database, Cosmos DB or Snowflake. Real-Time Intelligence handles streams with eventstreams and KQL eventhouses. Power BI's Direct Lake mode reads the Delta tables directly. Everything draws on capacity units from an F SKU: F64 gives 64. Background jobs are smoothed over 24 hours, and long overuse leads to throttling.
concepts.e: A team on an F64 capacity mirrors Azure SQL orders into OneLake, adds a shortcut to 2 TB of S3 clickstream, builds gold tables in a lakehouse notebook and serves a Direct Lake report without import refreshes.
concepts.c: What is the difference between a Fabric lakehouse and a Fabric warehouse, and when would you choose each?
concepts.i: Interviewers ask how OneLake, shortcuts and mirroring avoid copies, lakehouse versus warehouse, and how capacity, smoothing and throttling affect cost and scheduling.

concepts.title: Healthcare data standards: HL7 and FHIR
concepts.kw: healthcare interoperability hl7 v2 messages segments msh pid obx adt oru fhir resources patient encounter observation bundle profiles r4 r5 snomed ct loinc icd-10 terminology
concepts.s: Hospitals exchange data using HL7 standards. HL7 v2 sends pipe-delimited messages between systems, and FHIR offers resources such as Patient and Observation over a modern REST and JSON API.
concepts.d: HL7 v2 is still the workhorse inside hospitals: each message, such as ADT for admissions and transfers or ORU for lab results, is a set of segments like MSH, PID and OBX with fields split by pipes, and every site has local variations. FHIR models health data as resources (Patient, Encounter, Observation, Condition, MedicationRequest) that you read and write with REST calls, often grouped into Bundles. Profiles and implementation guides narrow resources for a country or use case. R4 is the most widely implemented version, R5 was published in 2023 and R6 is in development. Codes come from terminologies such as SNOMED CT, LOINC and ICD-10. India's ABDM, for example, exchanges health records as FHIR documents. For analytics, data engineers flatten resources into tables and map codes carefully.
concepts.e: A lab sends ORU messages with OBX segments for 1.2 million results a month. The pipeline converts them to FHIR Observations with LOINC codes, then flattens them into a table with one row per result, patient and date.
concepts.c: What is the main difference between how HL7 v2 and FHIR carry a patient's lab result?
concepts.i: Expect to compare HL7 v2 and FHIR, name key resources and terminologies, and explain how you would turn nested FHIR JSON into analytics tables while protecting patient privacy.

concepts.title: End-to-end exactly-once pipelines
concepts.kw: exactly once end to end replayable source checkpoint offsets idempotent sink transactional sink two-phase commit kafka transactions idempotent producer read_committed foreachbatch batch id effectively once
concepts.s: Exactly-once end to end means each input affects the final output once, even after crashes and retries. It needs three parts working together: a replayable source, checkpointed state and a sink that is idempotent or transactional.
concepts.d: Failures make engines replay data, so delivery is really at least once; exactly once is about effects. The source must be replayable from a position, such as Kafka offsets. The engine must save those positions and its state together in a checkpoint, so after a crash it restarts from a consistent point; Flink does this with checkpoint barriers, Spark with its checkpoint folder. The sink then needs one of two properties. An idempotent sink makes repeats harmless, such as an upsert by key or a Delta write tagged with a batch id that is skipped if already committed. A transactional sink commits output only when the checkpoint completes, such as Kafka transactions with consumers reading with read_committed, or Flink's two-phase commit. Side effects like emails or payments need their own idempotency keys.
concepts.e: A payments stream restarts after a crash and replays 12,000 events. The Delta sink skips the two micro-batches it already committed by batch id, so the daily total stays Rs 4.2 crore instead of double-counting.
concepts.c: Why does exactly-once processing inside Spark or Flink not guarantee exactly-once results in an external database?
concepts.i: Senior interviews want the three parts named, the difference between idempotent and transactional sinks, the latency cost of transactions and how you deal with external side effects.

concepts.title: LLM agents and tool use
concepts.kw: llm agents agentic loop plan act observe react tool use step limit planner executor multi-agent memory human approval least privilege trajectory evaluation task success rate
concepts.s: An LLM agent is a loop: the model chooses an action, such as calling a function, reads the result and decides the next step until the task is done. It suits open-ended tasks, but needs limits and checks.
concepts.d: Each turn the model sees the goal, the history and the result of its last action, then either calls another function or gives a final answer; this plan, act and observe pattern is often called ReAct. Designs range from one model with a few functions to a planner that hands steps to executors, or several specialised agents. Agents fail in new ways: they loop, pick the wrong function, invent arguments or let one early error snowball. So set a step and cost limit, give each function least privilege, keep actions that change data behind human approval, and log every step. Evaluate with task success rate on a fixed set of tasks, and read trajectories to see where runs go wrong. If a fixed workflow with one or two model calls does the job, prefer it: it is cheaper and easier to test.
concepts.e: An analytics agent answers "why did refunds rise last week?" with up to 8 steps: list tables, run 3 read-only SQL queries, chart the result and write a summary. On 50 test tasks it succeeded on 41, at about Rs 6 a task.
concepts.c: When would you choose a fixed workflow over an agent that decides its own steps?
concepts.i: Interviewers want the loop explained, the guardrails you add (step limits, least privilege, approvals, logging) and how you would measure success, plus when not to build an agent.

concepts.title: Streaming on Azure: Event Hubs and Stream Analytics
concepts.kw: azure event hubs namespace partitions consumer groups throughput units processing units kafka endpoint capture retention tiers basic standard premium dedicated stream analytics streaming units tumbling hopping windows
concepts.s: Azure Event Hubs ingests event streams and can act as a Kafka endpoint. Azure Stream Analytics runs SQL-like queries over those streams, and Capture writes them to the lake with no code.
concepts.d: An Event Hubs namespace holds event hubs, which are like Kafka topics. Each is split into partitions; events with the same partition key keep their order, and each consumer group reads independently. Tiers differ in capacity and retention: Basic and Standard buy throughput units, each about 1 MB/s or 1,000 events a second in, with retention up to 1 and 7 days; Premium and Dedicated use processing or capacity units, keep data up to 90 days and allow more partitions. Standard and above accept Kafka clients without code changes. Capture writes events to ADLS or Blob storage on a time or size window. Stream Analytics jobs query streams with SQL, tumbling, hopping, sliding and session windows, and scale with streaming units. Check current limits in Microsoft's docs before sizing.
concepts.e: Telemetry from 20,000 meters sends 5,000 events a second at 300 bytes, about 1.5 MB/s. A Standard namespace needs at least 5 throughput units for the event rate, with Capture writing 5-minute files to ADLS.
concepts.c: Why might a team point existing Kafka producers at Event Hubs instead of running their own Kafka cluster?
concepts.i: Expect to size throughput units from rate and size, explain partitions and consumer groups, compare Event Hubs with Kafka and Kinesis, and say when Stream Analytics is enough.

questions.q: How would you build an evaluation set for a new LLM support assistant?

p.t: Sample real questions from logs, with personal data removed
Cover categories and difficulty, including edge cases
Record expected answers or a rubric per item
Write labelling guidelines and check annotators agree

questions.a: I would sample real questions from production logs, removing personal data. I'd stratify them by category and difficulty and add expert edge cases, such as questions with no answer or attempts to break rules. For each item I'd record an expected answer or a short rubric. I'd write labelling guidelines and have two annotators label a sample to measure agreement before trusting the labels.

questions.q: Your team keeps improving scores on its golden set, but users say quality hasn't changed. What might be wrong?

p.t: Prompts were tuned on the test set, so it overfits
Keep a held-out split for final checks
The set no longer matches real traffic
Refresh it with recent production failures and version it

questions.a: The team has probably tuned on the golden set itself, so prompts overfit to those items and the scores leak into the design. I would keep a held-out split that nobody tunes against and use it for final checks. The set may also be stale and no longer match real traffic, because users now ask different things. I'd refresh it with recent production failures and version each change so scores stay comparable.

questions.q: Name the Azure services you would use for a batch pipeline from an operational database to a lake and a warehouse.

p.t: ADLS Gen2 as the lake storage
Data Factory to copy and schedule
Databricks, Synapse or Fabric to transform and serve
Purview, Entra ID and Key Vault for governance and secrets

questions.a: I'd land data in ADLS Gen2, which adds a hierarchical namespace to Blob storage. Azure Data Factory would copy from the database with a copy activity and schedule the pipeline. Transformation and serving would run in Azure Databricks, Synapse or Microsoft Fabric, depending on what the company already uses. Microsoft Purview would catalogue the data, Entra ID would control identity and Key Vault would keep connection secrets.

questions.q: You know AWS well. How would you explain the closest Azure equivalents of S3, Kinesis, Glue and Redshift?

p.t: S3 maps to ADLS Gen2 or Blob storage
Kinesis maps to Event Hubs
Glue maps to Data Factory, with Spark in Databricks or Synapse
Redshift maps to Synapse SQL pools or a Fabric warehouse

questions.a: S3 maps to ADLS Gen2, which is Blob storage with folders and access control. Kinesis maps to Event Hubs, which also accepts Kafka clients. Glue's orchestration and copy work maps to Azure Data Factory, with Spark jobs running in Databricks or Synapse. Redshift maps to Synapse dedicated SQL pools, though Microsoft now points new projects to a Fabric warehouse.

questions.q: Define loss ratio and combined ratio. What does a combined ratio of 105% tell you?

p.t: Loss ratio is incurred claims over earned premium
Incurred includes paid claims and reserve changes
Combined ratio adds the expense ratio
Above 100% means an underwriting loss

questions.a: The loss ratio is incurred claims divided by earned premium for the same period. Incurred claims are paid claims plus the change in reserves for outstanding claims. The combined ratio adds the expense ratio, covering expenses and commission. A combined ratio of 105% means an underwriting loss: the insurer pays 105 in claims and costs for every 100 of premium, before investment income.

questions.q: How is the expected claims cost of a motor policy usually modelled?

p.t: Pure premium is frequency times severity
Poisson GLM for claim counts
Gamma GLM for claim size
Exposure as an offset and rating factors as inputs

questions.a: The expected cost, or pure premium, is frequency times severity. Frequency is modelled with a Poisson GLM on claim counts, and severity with a gamma GLM on average claim size. Rating factors such as vehicle age, city and no-claim bonus are the inputs, and exposure in policy-years goes in as an offset, so a six-month policy isn't treated like a full year.

questions.q: You join an impressions stream to a clicks stream. How do you stop the join state growing forever?

p.t: Both sides are buffered in state waiting for matches
Add watermarks on both streams
Add a time-range condition to the join
Rows older than the watermark are dropped from state

questions.a: In a stream-stream join, both sides are buffered in state because a click may arrive after its impression. I'd add a watermark on each stream, saying how late events can be, and a time-range condition, for example a click must come within 30 minutes of the impression. With both, the engine knows when no new match is possible and can drop old rows from state, so it stays bounded.

questions.q: Orders must be converted to rupees using the exchange rate valid when each order happened. How would you join them in a stream?

p.t: Use a temporal join on event time
Rates are kept as a versioned table by key
Watermarks decide when a rate version is final
Late orders go to a side output or correction

questions.a: I'd use a temporal join on event time, so each order picks the rate valid as of its timestamp rather than the latest one. The rates stream would be kept as a versioned table, a changelog keyed by currency. Watermarks tell the engine when a version can no longer change, so results are emitted. Orders that arrive later than the watermark would go to a side output for a correction job.

questions.q: Explain how function calling works between an application and an LLM.

p.t: You describe functions with names and JSON schemas
The model returns a call with arguments, not prose
Your code runs the function, not the model
The result is sent back so the model can continue

questions.a: I describe each function with a name, a description and a JSON schema for its arguments. When the model wants one, it returns the function name and arguments instead of prose. My code then validates and executes the call, because the model never runs anything itself. I send the result back as a message, and the model continues, either calling another function or answering, in a loop.

questions.q: An LLM can call functions that query and update customer records. What guardrails would you put in place?

p.t: Allowlist functions and give least privilege
Validate arguments in code before running
Human approval before changes or payments
Log every call for audit

questions.a: I'd allowlist a small set of functions and give each least privilege, using read-only credentials for lookups. Arguments would be validated in code, for example with Pydantic, including checking the customer belongs to the signed-in user. Anything that updates records or moves money would need human approval in the interface. Every call would be logged with its arguments and result for audit.

questions.q: What are OneLake shortcuts and mirroring in Microsoft Fabric, and why do they matter?

p.t: OneLake is one lake per organisation
Shortcuts point at data in place without copying
Mirroring keeps a near real-time copy of a database
Tables are stored in open Delta format

questions.a: OneLake is a single lake for the whole tenant, built on ADLS Gen2. A shortcut points at data in place, in ADLS, S3 or Google Cloud Storage, without copying it, so many teams can read one source of truth. Mirroring replicates a database such as Azure SQL or Snowflake into OneLake continuously. Both land as open Delta tables, so Spark, SQL and Power BI read the same files.

questions.q: Your Fabric reports slow down every afternoon and some are rejected. How do you investigate and fix it?

p.t: Everything shares the capacity's capacity units
Overuse leads to smoothing then throttling
Use the Capacity Metrics app to find heavy items
Move or tune heavy jobs, or resize the capacity

questions.a: In Fabric every workload shares the capacity units of one F SKU, say an F64. Background jobs are smoothed over 24 hours, but if usage stays above the capacity, overage builds up and Fabric starts throttling, first delaying and then rejecting interactive requests. I'd open the Capacity Metrics app to find which items use the most units. Then I'd optimise or reschedule heavy refreshes and notebooks, move them to a separate capacity, or resize.

questions.q: Compare HL7 v2 and FHIR for a data engineer joining a hospital project.

p.t: HL7 v2 is pipe-delimited messages with segments
v2 has local variations at each site
FHIR uses resources over a REST JSON API
Codes come from terminologies such as LOINC and SNOMED

questions.a: HL7 v2 messages are pipe-delimited text made of segments, such as MSH for the header, PID for the patient and OBX for results, sent between hospital systems. Each site has local variations and custom Z-segments, so parsing needs mapping work. FHIR models data as resources like Patient and Observation, exchanged over a REST API as JSON. In both, the clinical meaning sits in codes from terminologies such as LOINC, SNOMED CT and ICD-10.

questions.q: How would you turn FHIR resources from several hospitals into tables for analytics?

p.t: Flatten nested resources into tables per resource type
Keep references between resources as keys
Map and standardise codes across sites
Protect patient identity with pseudonymised ids and access control

questions.a: I'd land the raw FHIR JSON, then flatten each resource type into its own table, for example one table for Observations with one row per result, using SQL on FHIR view definitions where they fit. References such as patient id and encounter id become keys that join the tables. Codes differ by site, so I'd map and standardise them to one terminology. Patient identifiers would be pseudonymised, with strict access control on the mapping.

questions.q: What do you need for exactly-once results from Kafka through Spark into a table?

p.t: A replayable source with offsets
Checkpoint offsets and state together
An idempotent or transactional sink
Skip or dedupe batches already committed

questions.a: First a replayable source: Kafka lets Spark re-read from stored offsets. Second, Spark must checkpoint those offsets and its state together, so a restart resumes from a consistent point. Third, the sink must be idempotent or transactional. With Delta in foreachBatch, I'd tag each write with the batch id so a batch that was already committed is skipped on replay, and the totals never double.

questions.q: Compare idempotent and transactional sinks for exactly-once delivery. What does each cost?

p.t: Idempotent sinks make repeated writes harmless
Transactional sinks commit with the checkpoint
Readers must read committed data only
Transactions add latency until each checkpoint

questions.a: An idempotent sink makes a repeated write harmless, for example an upsert on the same key, so replays don't change the result; it needs a natural key and a store that supports upserts. A transactional sink, such as Flink's two-phase commit into Kafka, writes inside a transaction and only commits on checkpoint. Consumers must use read_committed isolation or they will see aborted data. The cost is latency: output becomes visible only at each checkpoint interval.

questions.q: What is an LLM agent, and how is it different from a single LLM call?

p.t: A loop of choosing an action, acting and observing
The model chooses which function to call next
It stops at a final answer or a step limit
Errors can compound across steps

questions.a: An agent runs a loop: the model plans, calls a function, observes the result and decides the next step, which is the ReAct pattern. A single call just answers once. The agent keeps going until it gives a final answer or hits a step limit or cost budget. Because each step depends on the last, one early mistake can compound, so agents need more testing than a single call.

questions.q: How would you evaluate and make safe an agent that analyses company data with SQL?

p.t: Task success rate on a fixed set of tasks
Read trajectories to find where runs fail
Read-only access and least privilege
Limits on steps and cost, with human approval for changes

questions.a: I'd measure task success rate on a fixed set of 50 or so real analysis tasks with known answers. I'd also read trajectories, the step-by-step traces, to see where runs go wrong, such as a bad join. For safety the SQL runs with read-only credentials and least privilege on approved schemas. Each run has a step limit and cost limit, and anything that writes or emails needs human approval.

questions.q: How do partitions and consumer groups work in Azure Event Hubs?

p.t: An event hub is split into partitions
A partition key keeps related events in order
Consumer groups read the stream independently
Consumers checkpoint their position per partition

questions.a: An event hub is split into partitions, which spread the load. Producers set a partition key, such as device id, so events for that device land in one partition and stay in order. Each consumer group reads the whole stream independently, with its own position, so a dashboard and an archive job don't interfere. Readers checkpoint their offset per partition, usually in Blob storage, so they can resume after a restart.

questions.q: A team must move from self-run Kafka to Azure. Would you choose Event Hubs, and what would you check?

p.t: Event Hubs accepts Kafka clients on Standard and above
Size capacity units from throughput
Check retention and partition limits per tier
Check Kafka features in use are supported

questions.a: Event Hubs is a good fit because it exposes a Kafka endpoint on Standard and above, so existing Kafka clients mostly need only a new connection string. I'd size throughput units, about 1 MB a second in each on Standard, or processing units on Premium. I'd check retention, 7 days on Standard and up to 90 on Premium, and the partition limit per tier. Finally I'd check compatibility for the Kafka features the team uses, such as compaction or Kafka Streams.
